prerequisites: Elementary vector calculus. Concept of derivative and integral, with application to elementary functions.
System of linear equations and matrices.
Elementary concepts of particle kinematics and dynamics. Concept of force and Newton's principles. Work, kinetic and potential energy and energy conservation.
Kinematics and dynamics of the rigid body. Mass geometry. Moments of inertia.

learning_outcomes.text: Knowledge in basic and technological subjects, enabling them to learn new methods and theories, and providing them with versatility to adapt to new situations.
Ability to solve problems with initiative, decision-making, creativity, and critical reasoning.
Ability to communicate and transmit knowledge, skills, and abilities in the field of Industrial Engineering, both orally and in writing, and to all types of audiences.
Ability to handle specifications, regulations, and mandatory standards.
Ability to work in a team.
Understanding and mastery of basic concepts about the general laws of mechanics, thermodynamics, fields and waves, and electromagnetism and their application to solving engineering problems.
Knowledge of the principles of machine and mechanism theory.
Kinematically analyze and synthesize mechanisms.
Pose and solve the direct and inverse dynamic problem of a planar mechanism.
Analyze and design rigid and flexible transmissions.
Know widely applied mechanisms and understand that many apparently very different mechanisms respond to the same kinematic principles.
Perform kinematic diagrams of real mechanisms as a form of representation and understand the operation of the mechanism from said diagram.

Structurally analyze articulated mechanisms by criteria of nature and number of links or pairs, and by dimensional criteria, describing, as a result, the degrees of freedom or mobility of the mechanism and the existence or not of dead centers or return points and their singularities.
Know and develop the concepts, fundamentals, and methods applied for the kinematic and dynamic analysis of planar mechanisms.
Calculate velocities, accelerations, and forces in any planar mechanism, for specific positions of the mechanism and for complete cycles of movement.
Determine the type and dimensions of a bar mechanism to perform a specific function (problem known as mechanism synthesis).
Assimilate the relationships between the actions and the movement they produce in machines and be able to recognize the type of dynamic problem associated with each case.
Determine the inertia effects supported by the links or bars that make up the mechanisms.
Correctly include friction forces in sliding, rotational pairs, and rolling and analyze and understand the operation of friction-based mechanisms.
Know and define the key dimensions and characteristics of motion transmissions between rotating shafts (gears, belts, ...).
Determine transmission ratios in ordinary and epicyclic gear trains and know the preferred design criteria used to define the number of teeth.
Describe the role played by cam mechanisms, pointing out their advantages and disadvantages in relation to other mechanisms that achieve the same results.
Use software for the analysis, simulation, and design of machines and mechanisms.
Analyze and select information from various sources.
Develop the ability to understand and interpret the results obtained through kinematic and dynamic analysis of mechanisms and machines.

syllabus_topics: Theme 1. Mechanisms and machines. Basic concepts and schematization.
Definition, general structure and components of a machine
Classification of kinematic elements and pairs
Mobility of mechanisms: Grübler and Kutzbach criteria
Articulated quadrilateral and kinematic inversion. Grashof's Law
Theme 3. Analysis of velocities and accelerations.
Method of relative velocities and accelerations.
Direct dynamic analysis on reduced mechanisms
Flywheels: Steady state, degree of irregularity, concept of GD2
Friction due to sliding, in rotational pairs and in rolling.
Concept of balancing. Balancing of mechanisms.
Theme 9. Introduction to rigid motion transmissions.
Fundamentals, terminology and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Theme 11. Helical cylindrical, bevel and worm-gear drives.
Fundamentals, terminology and classification. Forces. Variation of center distance. Interference
Ordinary and epicyclic trains. Willis's Formula.
Fundamental design law and kinematics of cams.
teaching_methods: Laboratory / field / computer lab / language lab practices

assessment_methods.method: Continuous Assessment (EC) - Problems completed in classroom practices and/or tasks proposed by professors.
Laboratory Practices (PL) - Preparation, attitude, submission of a report sheet, and knowledge evaluation via multiple-choice tests.
Final Exam (EF) - Conceptual questions, quick problem-solving, and complex problems.

assessment_rules: For the ordinary and June extraordinary calls, the final grade is calculated as EC + PL + EF, provided a minimum of 3 points out of 7.5 is achieved on the Final Exam. If this minimum is not met, the course cannot be passed, and the grade recorded will be 4.9. For the January extraordinary and differentiated evaluations, the assessment consists of a single written exam, where 9 points are for the subject's curriculum and 1 point for laboratory content. A minimum of 5 points out of 10 is required to pass the single written exam.
